title: Scaling laws: what the curves really say, from Kaplan to Chinchilla
summary: What a scaling curve actually plots and what it never claimed: power-law fits of loss against parameters, data and compute, the Kaplan allocation and the Chinchilla correction (and the still-disputed reason they differed), what the curves can't see — capabilities, emergence, repeated data — and how labs like OpenAI and Meta use small runs to budget a big one.

topics: deep dive: scaling laws — what the curves really say
concepts_taught: neural scaling laws as power-law fits of pre-training cross-entropy loss against parameters, tokens and compute (C ≈ 6ND): straight lines on log-log axes, steady but diminishing returns (Kaplan: doubling parameters cuts loss by a factor of about 0.95), over a measured range, with a floor because language has non-zero entropy — and Kaplan's own section 6.3 saying the laws must break down

compute-optimal allocation and the Chinchilla correction: Kaplan's N ∝ C^0.73 (big models stopped early) versus Chinchilla's equal scaling of parameters and tokens, found by IsoFLOP valleys and a parametric loss fit; the ~20 tokens-per-parameter rule as arithmetic on Chinchilla's table; and the still-disputed cause of the gap (learning-rate schedule vs. non-embedding counting at small scale vs. last-layer cost, warmup and optimizer tuning), plus the Besiroglu replication of the third method

what scaling curves cannot see: loss is not capability; emergent abilities (Wei) versus the metric-artifact account (Schaeffer: exact-match scoring turns smooth per-token gains into cliffs); inverse-scaling reversals; and data-constrained scaling (repeated data roughly as good as unique up to about four epochs)

how labs budget a run with scaling laws: fit small runs and extrapolate (GPT-4 loss from ≤10,000x less compute; Llama 3 IsoFLOPs to 10^22 extrapolated to 3.8×10^25, flatter valleys making exact size forgiving), a separate two-step mapping from loss to benchmark accuracy, and inference-aware over-training of models meant to be served (Sardana; Llama 3's smaller models)

lore.note: Alan's February 2024 private call that AI progress would flatten developed rather than restated: rereading Kaplan for the scaling-laws deep dive, he located the error — not pessimism but a reading mistake, forecasting capabilities off a curve that only measures loss (the bend he feared is real, in Kaplan's section 6.3, on the loss axis). He still refuses to say anything changed his mind; he says writing his falsifier down would have exposed the axis swap.
